title: Working It Out: A Conversation About Communication Skills

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: Can I pick your brain about something? I have a big presentation coming up and I'm terrified. I always freeze or rush through the slides and then nobody asks questions, which makes me feel like I've completely failed.

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: The no-questions thing is interesting, isn't it? It doesn't necessarily mean it went badly. Sometimes it means it was very clear, so there was nothing to ask. But I take your point — it can feel that way.

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: You've given loads of presentations, haven't you? What's your secret?

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: Honestly? The first thing is slowing down. When you're nervous, you rush. And rushing makes you harder to follow, which increases anxiety, which makes you rush more. It's a vicious cycle. So the single most useful thing is to deliberately breathe before you start and between each main point.

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: I know that's good advice. But in the moment I just can't seem to do it.

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: That's because you're trying to do it in the moment. You need to practise it in low-stakes situations first — casual conversations, small meetings. Basically, you're training a new habit. You can't suddenly perform a behaviour you've never practised under pressure.

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: Signpost everything. Tell your audience where you're going and where you've been. "First I'll cover…" "So, to sum up that section…" "Now, moving on to…" It sounds obvious, but it makes an enormous difference. When people know what structure to expect, they can follow even complex content.

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: I tend to assume people are following me. Maybe I'm wrong to do that.

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: You probably are. You know your material — they're encountering it fresh. What's obvious to you isn't obvious to them. And I'd add: don't be afraid of silence. A pause feels much longer to you than it does to the audience. Use it.

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: I've heard that. It's harder than it sounds, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: Absolutely. But it gets easier. The other thing — and this one is underrated — is eye contact. Not scanning nervously, not staring at your slides. Making actual contact with individual people in the room. It's connecting, not performing.

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: What about questions? I'm always worried I won't know the answer.

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: Well, you don't have to know everything. "That's a really good question — I'd need to look into that" is a completely valid response. What you should avoid is making up an answer you're not sure about. That's where credibility gets damaged.

dialogue.speaker: Selin
dialogue.text: That's really reassuring. So it's about communicating, not performing. I think I've been thinking about it the wrong way.

dialogue.speaker: James
dialogue.text: Exactly. The audience wants you to succeed. They're on your side. If you can just connect with them rather than trying to impress them, most presentations go much better than expected.

vocab.definition: to guide an audience through the structure of a presentation or speech using explicit phrases
